short: Run coding agents on Agent Substrate, in your organization's cluster
long:
Run Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents in a Kubernetes cluster that runs
Agent Substrate, with DefenseClaw guarding every tool call, model call and network
request the same way it does on a laptop. The agent works on a copy of your folder
inside a sandbox in the cluster; no keys are in it. It keeps running when you
detach, and you can come back from any machine.

Sign in once with "defenseclaw substrate login", then run "defenseclaw substrate run claude"
in a project folder. These commands need no local DefenseClaw install.

short: Administer people's access to the cluster (administrators)
End every sign-in of a person, list the ended ones, or lift an end
long:
--user PERSON ends every token of that person issued before now, on every device, and closes their open
terminals (PERSON is a principal such as bob@example.com, or issuer#subject to end the sign-ins of a person who
has not signed in yet). A refresh token the person holds can still get new tokens from the sign-in server: to
lock someone out, also end their sessions there. --list shows the people whose sign-ins are ended. --lift --user
PERSON removes an end early; it is audited.

short: List what your agents are waiting for you to approve
long:
Lists the questions your agents asked that nobody has answered yet. Answer with
"defenseclaw substrate approve ID" or "defenseclaw substrate reject ID". An agent attached to your
terminal shows the same question on its last line. An unattended run (--task, --batch)
denies its asks unless its profile sets unattended_asks: queue; a queued ask is marked
"unattended" in the RUN column and is denied when its time runs out.

With --standing it lists the approvals given with "approve --always" that are still in force:
the agent, the host, what the approval covers, who approved it and when. Take one back with
"defenseclaw substrate revoke NAME HOST".

short: Send a signed policy bundle to the cluster, or see what is in force (administrators)
long:
A policy bundle is a signed file your organization's policy tooling makes. Administrators send it to the cluster
with "bundle apply" and read which bundles are in force with "bundle status". The cluster checks the signature; this
command only sends the file as it is.

short: Send a signed policy bundle to the cluster
long:
Sends the bundle file to the cluster as it is (up to 48 KiB). With --atespaces the bundle applies to those groups
of agents only; without it, to the whole cluster. With --dry-run it only checks that the file can be read and is not
empty, and sends nothing. Needs an administrator sign-in.
example:
defenseclaw substrate bundle apply policy.bundle
defenseclaw substrate bundle apply policy.bundle --atespaces team-a,team-b --dry-run

bundle signed with a key revoked since is refused. Running it again puts the newer bundle back. Needs an administrator
sign-in.

short: Save the agent's work so you can undo back to it
long:
Saves a restore point of the agent's folder inside the agent, then has the cluster store a snapshot of
the agent (it pauses for a few seconds), so the restore point survives a crash of the agent's worker.
"defenseclaw substrate undo NAME" goes back to the last one; after a crash it first brings the agent back to
that snapshot. With --every 1h it saves one on that schedule for as long as the command runs.
example:
defenseclaw substrate checkpoint fix-tests-7f3a
defenseclaw substrate checkpoint fix-tests-7f3a --every 1h

short: Come back to an agent and put it on this terminal
long:
Attaches your terminal to a running or suspended agent from any machine you are signed in on.
A suspended agent wakes in about a fifth of a second and shows the screen as you left it. Press Ctrl-]
to detach again. If the connection drops, it reconnects by itself. NAME is the name "defenseclaw substrate list"
shows, or the --name you gave run when only one agent has it.

With --mcp NAME=COMMAND (Preview, repeatable) the agent can use an MCP server that runs on this computer, while this
command is attached. See "defenseclaw substrate run --help". An agent that is already running reads its MCP servers
when it starts, so start a new session in it to see NAME.
example:
defenseclaw substrate connect fix-tests-7f3a
defenseclaw substrate connect fix-tests

many snapshots each agent had. Pull the changes first with "defenseclaw substrate pull":
what is not pulled is gone.

short: Check that this computer can run agents in the cluster
long:
Checks, from this computer, everything a run needs: the cluster is set up here, its admin address answers
over TLS, you are signed in and the cluster accepts it, the sign-in server matches, attach through the gateway works and
you have what it asks for, your sign-in can be kept safely, the cluster can check ended sign-ins (for administrators: whether
it ends them at all), and (for administrators, when the cluster uses signed policy bundles) every stage's bundle still verifies. Nothing needs to be installed here, and nothing in the
cluster changes.

Administrators add the cluster's own checks (version, issuer, snapshot bucket, access policies, egress callout, router
clients, routes, API access) with --install-file, the SubstrateInstall file you gave ate-setup: they are read with
kubectl and your own cloud credentials, the same as defenseclaw substrate verify. --cluster without it says what is missing.

The last line is "ready for agents" when no check failed and the cluster components (gateway, leader, controller,
callout) were checked, which needs --install-file. Without it the last line says that the checks on this computer pass
and that the cluster components were not checked. Otherwise it is "not ready" and each failed check says how to fix
it, and the exit code is 1.
example:
defenseclaw substrate doctor
defenseclaw substrate doctor --cluster --json

short: Sign in to a cluster
long:
Signs you in to the cluster your organization runs, with your own account. It prints a web
address and a short code; open the address in any browser, enter the code and approve. Your
sign-in is kept in the system keychain, never in a file you can read. The first time, give the cluster
address with --admin-url (your administrator has it); the cluster tells the launcher which sign-in server to
use. After that, "defenseclaw substrate login" alone renews the sign-in.

On a cluster that has no sign-in server (an open-source install), use --kube: you are then the Kubernetes user of
your current kubeconfig, and nothing is stored.

In CI, use --workload (or set DEFENSECLAW_SUBSTRATE_WORKLOAD_TOKEN_FILE): the run is then attributed to the
pipeline's own identity, with a GitHub Actions token or a projected Kubernetes token minted for the cluster's workload audience, and nothing is stored.
example:
defenseclaw substrate login --admin-url https://admin.example.test:9443
defenseclaw substrate login --admin-url https://admin.example.test:9443 --issuer https://sso.example.test/realms/corp --client-id defenseclaw-launcher
defenseclaw substrate login
defenseclaw substrate login --workload --workload-token-file /var/run/secrets/ci/token

short: Sign out of a cluster: end the sign-in there and forget it
long:
Ends your sign-in on the cluster, so a copy of its token stops working there, then ends it at the sign-in server
where that server supports it, and removes the stored sign-in. --all ends every token of yours issued before now, on
every device, and closes their open terminals. An end covers tokens already issued: a refresh token held on another
device or in a copied store can still get new ones, so also end your sessions at the sign-in server (ask your
administrator). Your agents keep running; sign in again to reach them.

example: defenseclaw substrate logs -f fix-tests-7f3a

long:

running the current kit and the one before it; "migrate" moves an agent that is older than
that onto the current kit without losing its work.

short: Clear a policy conflict on an agent (administrators only)
long:
For administrators. When something outside DefenseClaw keeps rewriting an agent's network policy,
three reverts in ten minutes mark the agent policy_conflict and put it on deny-only: it keeps only the
DefenseClaw rule, and each later change by the other writer is replaced with deny-only again, so a foreign
policy never stays in force. Once the other writer is stopped, "reset" clears that state so the controller
writes the full policy again. Name the agent as ATESPACE/NAME. The reset is recorded in the audit log under
your own name.
example: defenseclaw substrate policy reset eng-web/fix-tests-7f3a --reason "removed the GitOps rule"

short: Open an agent's dev server in your browser (port forward)
long:
Forwards a port the agent's app listens on (127.0.0.1:PORT inside the agent) to 127.0.0.1:LOCAL on this
computer, so you can open http://127.0.0.1:LOCAL in your browser. LOCAL is PORT unless you give PORT:LOCAL; when PORT
is taken here, the next free port is used. The forward listens on 127.0.0.1 only and only you can open it. It stays
in the foreground until you press Ctrl-C.

Ports 1024-65535 can be forwarded, except the relay's own port; your administrator can allow fewer or turn port
forwarding off. Every forward is recorded in the cluster's audit log. The forwarded app runs as "localhost" in your
browser, like any local dev server: open only apps you trust there.
example:
defenseclaw substrate port web-3f2a 3000
defenseclaw substrate port web-3f2a 3000:8000 5173

short: Review what the agent changed and bring it home
long:
Reads the agent's work back to this machine and shows what changed, with the files that need a
careful look first (scripts, CI and hook files, dotfiles, secrets in the text, large or binary files,
links that leave the folder, agent settings, MCP servers, shell startup files). Nothing touches your folder
until you choose: --apply writes the changes into the folder, --branch NAME puts them on a new git branch,
--patch-out FILE writes a patch. --push-branch NAME (Preview) pushes the agent's work from inside the
agent to its checkout's origin as a new branch, with the credential the cluster adds for that host; it
asks first unless your profile allows it, and never forces.

When a change can run code on this machine, --apply asks first (the default answer is no). --yes takes
that safe answer, so --apply --yes writes nothing and says why; after you reviewed the flagged files,
--allow-flagged writes them too.

On the computer you started the agent from, it compares the changes with the folder you sent. On
another computer, run it in a git checkout of that folder: it compares the agent's work with the
checkout's last commit, so files sent that were not committed show as added. That computer cannot know
what run left out with --exclude, so repeat it (--exclude GLOB, once for each) or say there was none
(--no-exclude) before --apply or --branch; until then they refuse, and --patch-out still works.
example:
defenseclaw substrate pull fix-tests-7f3a
defenseclaw substrate pull fix-tests-7f3a --branch agent/fix-tests
defenseclaw substrate pull fix-tests-7f3a --push-branch agent/fix-tests

short: Send your newer changes into a running agent (Preview)
long:
Sends the changes you made in this folder since the last send (the run or an earlier push) into the
agent's copy. Paths limit it to those files or folders. The rules of run apply: secret files are held
back (share one with --unmask), --exclude holds more back, and the cluster's upload limit counts.

Before it writes, it saves a restore point: "defenseclaw substrate undo NAME --to N" goes back to it.
When the agent also changed a file you changed, nothing is sent and the files are listed (exit 3).
Then choose: --mine sends yours (the agent's version stays in the restore point), --theirs keeps the
agent's and sends the rest, and --patch-out FILE keeps the agent's and writes your change to FILE.
When sending yours would remove an agent file or folder in its way (a file where you made a folder, or
a folder where you made a file), --mine names it and sends nothing; add --replace to send yours anyway.
What you send is not shown as the agent's work in a later pull. This command is a Preview.
example:
defenseclaw substrate push fix-tests-7f3a
defenseclaw substrate push fix-tests-7f3a src/app.py --mine

short: Let the agent's relay get a new certificate; bring a crashed agent back
long:
Clears the cluster's record of the agent's relay certificate, so the relay's next request
gets a first certificate and no certificate issued before it can renew. Use it when
"defenseclaw substrate connect" fails because the relay restarted inside the agent, or after an
emergency relay CA rotation, while substrate.relay_cert_reissue is refuse (the managed default).
A crashed agent is also brought back to its last snapshot, as "defenseclaw substrate undo" does;
what it did after that snapshot is lost, so it asks first. Only the agent's owner or an
administrator can run it.
example: defenseclaw substrate recover fix-tests-7f3a

short: Take back an approval given with --always
long:
Takes back what "defenseclaw substrate approve --always" allowed for one agent and host: the agent's
next request to the host asks you again. The cluster drops the host from the agent's network rules
within about a minute. List the approvals in force with "defenseclaw substrate approvals --standing".
An administrator names another person's agent as ATESPACE/NAME; the revoke is recorded under their
own name.
example: defenseclaw substrate revoke fix-tests-7f3a registry.example.test

short: Run a coding agent in the cluster on a copy of this folder
long:
Starts the coding agent in a sandbox in the cluster, on a copy of the current folder (secret
files such as .env and keys are held back), and puts the agent on your terminal. The agent is claude,
codex, copilot, opencode, hermes, kiro, antigravity, cursor-agent, amp or devin. The agents that sign in to a
vendor account (kiro, antigravity, cursor-agent, amp, devin) start in open source only after you say yes to a
warning (or pass --yes), because the sign-in token stays in the agent and its snapshots; a managed cluster refuses them. A banner shows the guard profile, model, allowed hosts and how to leave. When the
guard asks before a step, the question appears on the last line: press Ctrl-\ to answer once, always or deny.

Press Ctrl-] to detach; the agent keeps running and suspends when idle. Come back from any machine with
"defenseclaw substrate connect NAME". Bring the changes home with "defenseclaw substrate pull NAME".

With --task the agent runs headless without you: asks are denied, or queued for approval when the profile's
unattended_asks is queue, and the run is checked as strictly as an unattended job. Add --detach to leave it
running and follow it with "defenseclaw substrate logs -f NAME".
With --batch FILE every task gets its own agent on the same folder; --parallel limits how many run at once.
With --clone URL the agent starts from a repository instead of a copy of the folder. With --clone . (Preview)
it starts from this checkout: the agent fetches the branch's history from its remote, and only the unpushed
commits and uncommitted changes are sent from here. Arguments after -- go to the agent.

With --mcp NAME=COMMAND (Preview, repeatable) the agent can use an MCP server that runs on this computer. This command
starts COMMAND when the agent opens the server NAME and carries its messages through the cluster while this command is
attached; every tool call goes through the cluster's guard first. COMMAND is split like a shell would split it, with
quotes and backslashes only, and runs without a shell. NAME is a-z, 0-9, _ and -, up to 32 characters. --mcp does not
go with --detach or --batch.
example:
defenseclaw substrate run claude
defenseclaw substrate run codex --task "fix the failing tests" --detach

short: Manage the secrets your agents may use (values never enter an agent)
long:
A secret is a key an agent can use without ever seeing it: the cluster adds the real value
to requests to the hosts the secret is bound to. These commands list the names you can use,
store your own, and remove or test them. Values are never shown.

short: Add a secret of your own for one host, under a template
long:
Creates your own secret NAME for HOST under TEMPLATE (see secrets templates) and stores its
value. A host the template covers is used from your agents' next request; any other host waits
until an administrator approves it. For a basic template (git hosts, PyPI) give only the token:
the cluster adds the user name. generic-basic needs --user.

The value comes from exactly one source: the terminal without echo (no flag), --from-gh (the
GitHub CLI's sign-in), --from-keychain SERVICE (macOS keychain), --from-op op://vault/item/field
(1Password CLI), --from-file PATH, --stdin or --from-env VAR. It is never put on a command line
and never printed.
example:
defenseclaw substrate secrets add gl-work --template gitlab --host gitlab.com --from-op op://eng/gitlab/token
defenseclaw substrate secrets add nexus --template generic-basic --host nexus.corp.example --user ci-bot --from-file ~/.nexus-token

short: Add DefenseClaw's settings to the SubstrateInstall file (administrators)
long:
Reads the SubstrateInstall document you give to ate-setup and adds the settings DefenseClaw needs: the egress
callout, the router client the gateway attaches launchers through, and, only when you say your Substrate build has them,
the callout body opt-in and the long-stream timeouts. It refuses when Substrate already sends egress to another callout,
and says what to do. Nothing here changes the cluster. With --issuer it reads, with kubectl when it can, the key set the
gateway verifies actor tokens with (--keys-url, the idp Service by default) and warns when it does not answer.

The result is written next to the file as FILE.new (mode 0600) for you to read. With --yes it replaces the file and keeps
the old one as FILE.bak. With --dry-run it only shows the changes. With --remove it takes DefenseClaw's settings out again.

With --print-access-policies and --plan FILE it prints the access policies the install would write, as commands and
manifests a global owner can apply, and reads no install file.

Next: run ate-setup deploy with the new file, then install the chart with helm install.

With --overlay-only (also spelled --no-chart) the chart belongs to Argo CD or Flux, not to this command. It makes the same
checks and writes the same file, and then names the chart values the overlay assumes so the values in your repo can match.
It never runs helm. The next step is to commit the file and let ate-setup deploy apply it.
example:
defenseclaw substrate setup --install-file install.yaml --namespace defenseclaw --dry-run
defenseclaw substrate setup --install-file install.yaml --capability route-timeouts --yes
defenseclaw substrate setup --install-file install.yaml --overlay-only --issuer https://cluster-a.example --yes
defenseclaw substrate setup --print-access-policies --plan plan.json

short: Show who you are signed in as, or one agent or batch in detail
long:
Without a name, shows the cluster and account in use and how many agents you have.
With a name, shows that agent: where it runs, which profile guards it and its batch.
With --batch, shows every agent of a batch run.

For administrators, --cluster shows the health of the whole setup: gateway, leader, controller and callout,
the agents and templates in the cluster (agents by state, also per launcher and managed atespace), the agents
in policy_conflict per atespace and the setup checks. It reads the cluster with kubectl (give --install-file),
and the agents in policy_conflict with your DefenseClaw sign-in (sign in as an administrator, or the count is
unknown).
Exit 75 means the cluster could not be reached; there is no document.

short: Keep sending your changes into a running agent while you work (Preview)
long:
Watches this folder and sends each change into the agent's copy, one way, until Ctrl-C, --for, or
the agent is deleted. It sends 1 second after the last change, and at most 5 seconds after the first.
Each batch follows the rules of push: secret files are held back, ignored files, .git and package
caches are not sent, and a file the agent also changed keeps the agent's version (it is named once;
send yours with push NAME --mine FILE). It saves a restore point at the start, then one every
10 minutes in which something was sent. A suspended agent is not woken: changes wait until it is back.
Nothing keeps running after it stops. --watch is required. This command is a Preview.
example:
defenseclaw substrate sync fix-tests-7f3a --watch
defenseclaw substrate sync fix-tests-7f3a --watch --for 2h

short: Build, check and publish actor images with their attestation (administrators)
long:
Administrators build the images agents run in, check that an image would be admitted, scan one, publish it to the
registry the cluster pulls from, and make the signing key. These commands run on this computer and need no sign-in.

  build     build an image from a base image and push it with its attestation
  verify    check an image's attestation
  scan      scan an image
  publish   copy a verified image to the cluster's registry
  keygen    make a signing key pair

Run defenseclaw substrate template COMMAND --help for the flags.

short: Build an actor image from a base image and push it with its attestation
long:
Builds a coding-agent image for the cluster from a base image: adds the DefenseClaw hook and relay, scans what is
inside, and pushes it with a signed attestation that the cluster checks before it runs the image.

Usage: defenseclaw substrate template build --from IMAGE --to REPO:TAG --hook-binary FILE --relay-binary FILE --key FILE [flags]

Flags:
  --connector NAME                connector to build: claudecode, codex, opencode, copilot, hermes, kiro, antigravity,
                                  cursor, amp or devin (default claudecode)
  --from IMAGE                    base image (the OpenShell harness image for the connector, with tmux)
  --to REPO:TAG                   target repository and tag
  --kit-version VERSION           kit version (default dev)
  --hook-binary FILE              defenseclaw-actor-hook (linux static)
  --relay-binary FILE             defenseclaw-actor-relay (linux static)
  --key FILE                      attestation private key (PEM, mode 0600); not needed with --dry-run
  --anchors FILE                  trust anchors, to let an attested base count as trusted
  --allow-unverified-base         build on a base that is not trusted (the cluster will refuse it by default)
  --block-at LEVEL                lowest finding severity that blocks the build: critical, high, medium, low or none (default high)
  --policy-generation N           policy generation recorded in the attestation (default 1)
  --builder-id ID                 builder id recorded in the attestation
  --provider NAME                 model route (claudecode: bedrock or anthropic; codex: bedrock or openai; default from substrate.llm.providers)
  --model ID                      default model id
  --gateway-url URL               actor listener URL (default http://<substrate.services.actor> of --config)
  --fail-mode MODE                interactive outage mode: open or closed
  --task-stall DURATION           end a --task run that makes no progress for this long (1m to 24h; default 10m)
  --no-mcp-static                 do not run mcp-scanner over tool descriptions
  --mcp-analyzers LIST            mcp-scanner analyzers (default yara)
  --keep-entrypoint               keep the base image ENTRYPOINT and CMD (tests; a real actor image starts the relay)
  --dry-run                       scan the composed image and stop before pushing
  --trusted-base sha256:DIGEST    base image digest the admin trusts (repeatable)
  --mcp-host HOST                 remote MCP host that is allowed (repeatable)
  --session-key FILE              the gateway's relay session public key (public.pem of the relay session Secret);
                                  KID=FILE is checked against the key's own id (repeatable)
  --session-issuer URL            iss of the session tokens the keys verify (default https://<substrate.services.admin>
                                  of --config, the issuer the gateway signs with)
  --session-audience AUD          aud of the session tokens (default: the one the gateway signs)
  --verify-url URL                gateway URL the relay checks each session token with (default
                                  the relay verify endpoint of <gateway-url>; --session-key keys are checked first)

Flags build, verify, scan and publish all take:
  --json                          print JSON
  --insecure-registry HOST:PORT   registry reached over plain HTTP (repeatable)
  --registry-user USER            registry user
  --registry-password-file FILE   file with the registry password
  --registry-auth-host HOST       registry or token host that gets the login (repeatable; build adds the --to host,
                                  never the --from host)
  --config FILE                   DefenseClaw config.yaml (scanner and admission settings)
  --platform OS/ARCH              image platform (default linux/amd64)

Exit code: 0 built, 1 blocked, 2 usage error.
example: defenseclaw substrate template build --connector claudecode --from REGISTRY/base:TAG --to REGISTRY/actor:TAG --hook-binary hook --relay-binary relay --key attestation.key

short: Make a signing key pair for attestations
long:
Makes a signing key pair for attestations: attestation.key (private, mode 0600; keep it in the cluster Secret) and
attestation.pub (the trust anchor).

Usage: defenseclaw substrate template keygen --out DIR [flags]

Flags:
  --out DIR                       directory for attestation.key and attestation.pub; required
  --json                          print JSON

Exit code: 0 done, 2 usage error.
example: defenseclaw substrate template keygen --out ./keys

short: Copy a verified image to the cluster's registry
long:
Copies a verified image, and its attestation, to the registry the cluster pulls from. It verifies first and refuses an
image that would not be admitted. With --template it then creates the ActorTemplate that runs the image, pinned by its
digest, so the image can be started with "defenseclaw substrate run --template NAME".

Usage: defenseclaw substrate template publish SOURCE@DIGEST TARGET:TAG --anchors FILE [flags]

Flags:
  --anchors FILE                  trust anchors (PEM bundle of public keys); required
  --min-policy-generation N       refuse attestations scanned under an older policy generation (default 0)
  --dry-run                       verify the image and print what would be copied and created; change nothing
  --template ATESPACE/NAME        create the ActorTemplate from the published image
  --class CLASS                   sandbox class: gvisor or microvm (default gvisor)
  --cpu CPU                       cpu limit, for example 1500m or 2 (default 1500m)
  --memory SIZE                   memory limit, for example 1536Mi or 2Gi (default 1536Mi)
  --workdir DIR                   the image decides its working directory (/work in the kit images); only that value is accepted
  --env K=V                       non-secret environment variable for the container (repeatable)
  --worker-label K=V              label a worker pool must carry (repeatable; replaces the label that --class selects)
  --api-address HOST:PORT         ate-api-server address (default substrate.api.address)
  --api-server-name NAME          TLS name of ate-api-server (default substrate.api.server_name)
  --api-ca-file FILE              CA bundle for ate-api-server's certificate (default substrate.api.ca_file)
  --api-token-file FILE           bearer token file (default substrate.api.token_file)
  --api-auth MODE                 serviceaccount or mtls (default substrate.api.auth)

Flags build, verify, scan and publish all take:
  --json                          print JSON
  --insecure-registry HOST:PORT   registry reached over plain HTTP (repeatable)
  --registry-user USER            registry user
  --registry-password-file FILE   file with the registry password
  --registry-auth-host HOST       registry or token host that gets the login (repeatable; build adds the --to host,
                                  never the --from host)
  --config FILE                   DefenseClaw config.yaml (scanner and admission settings)
  --platform OS/ARCH              image platform (default linux/amd64)

The --template flags need --template. The --api-* flags override the substrate.api section of the file given by --config.

A template cannot be changed once created. If ATESPACE/NAME already has this image and these settings, nothing happens
("already up to date"). If it has another image or other settings, a new template NAME-<first 8 hex of the digest> is
created and its name is printed: give that name to "run --template". No template is ever deleted.

Exit code: 0 published, 1 not published (or the API refused the template), 2 usage error, 75 the Substrate API cannot be
reached (run the same command again).
example: defenseclaw substrate template publish SOURCE@sha256:DIGEST TARGET:TAG --anchors attestation.pub

short: Scan an image for risky skills, MCP servers and plugins
long:
Scans an image the way a build does (skills, MCP servers, plugins and the hook files) and prints the verdict. It
changes nothing.

Usage: defenseclaw substrate template scan IMAGE [flags]

Flags:
  --no-mcp-static                 do not run mcp-scanner over tool descriptions
  --mcp-analyzers LIST            mcp-scanner analyzers (default yara)
  --block-at LEVEL                lowest finding severity that blocks: critical, high, medium, low or none (default high)
  --connector NAME                check the kit's hook files and switches for this connector: claudecode, codex,
                                  opencode, copilot, hermes, kiro, antigravity, cursor, amp or devin
  --mcp-host HOST                 remote MCP host that is allowed (repeatable)

Flags build, verify, scan and publish all take:
  --json                          print JSON
  --insecure-registry HOST:PORT   registry reached over plain HTTP (repeatable)
  --registry-user USER            registry user
  --registry-password-file FILE   file with the registry password
  --registry-auth-host HOST       registry or token host that gets the login (repeatable; build adds the --to host,
                                  never the --from host)
  --config FILE                   DefenseClaw config.yaml (scanner and admission settings)
  --platform OS/ARCH              image platform (default linux/amd64)

Exit code: 0 clean, 1 blocked, 2 usage error.
example: defenseclaw substrate template scan REGISTRY/actor@sha256:DIGEST --connector claudecode

short: Check an image's attestation the way the cluster does
long:
Checks the attestation of an image the way the cluster does, and says whether it would be admitted.

Usage: defenseclaw substrate template verify IMAGE --anchors FILE [flags]

Flags:
  --anchors FILE                  trust anchors (PEM bundle of public keys); required
  --min-policy-generation N       refuse attestations scanned under an older policy generation (default 0)
  --max-age DURATION              refuse attestations older than this, for example 720h (default 0, no limit)
  --allow-unverified-base         admit a template built on an untrusted base
  --allow-tag                     accept a tag reference (it can move; pin by digest in templates)
  --revoke KEYID                  key id to refuse (repeatable)

Flags build, verify, scan and publish all take:
  --json                          print JSON
  --insecure-registry HOST:PORT   registry reached over plain HTTP (repeatable)
  --registry-user USER            registry user
  --registry-password-file FILE   file with the registry password
  --registry-auth-host HOST       registry or token host that gets the login (repeatable; build adds the --to host,
                                  never the --from host)
  --config FILE                   DefenseClaw config.yaml (scanner and admission settings)
  --platform OS/ARCH              image platform (default linux/amd64)

Exit code: 0 admitted, 1 not admitted, 2 usage error.
example: defenseclaw substrate template verify REGISTRY/actor@sha256:DIGEST --anchors attestation.pub

short: Put the agent's folder back to a restore point
long: Goes back to the last restore point (or --to ID) inside the agent and discards what the agent changed since. It asks first. After a crash it first brings the agent back to its last snapshot; a --task agent this computer started whose task was lost then starts that task again from the beginning, on a fresh copy of its folder.

short: Show what your agents used: model calls, tokens and cost
long:
Shows the model use of your agents and what it cost, rolled up by agent (the default),
model, batch, atespace, day, connector or provider. You see only your own use; an
administrator adds --all for everyone and --by person for one line per person.
Calls whose model is not in the price table show no cost and are not in the total.
example:
defenseclaw substrate usage
  defenseclaw substrate usage --by model --since 24h
  defenseclaw substrate usage --all --by person

flags.usage: only this batch

short: Check the cluster setup: issuer, snapshot bucket, access grants, callout and version
long:
For administrators. Checks that the cluster is set up as DefenseClaw needs it: Substrate's version is
one DefenseClaw is tested on, the cluster has its own sign-in issuer, the snapshot bucket is private and
encrypted, DefenseClaw holds the right access grants, the egress callout is registered and nobody else
can reach agents through the router, and no agent is in policy_conflict. It reads the cluster with kubectl,
the snapshot bucket with your own aws or gcloud CLI, and the agents in policy_conflict with your DefenseClaw
sign-in (--context; sign in as an administrator, or the count is unknown and the check warns).

Exit 0: every check passed or warned. Exit 1: a check failed. Exit 2: wrong arguments. Exit 75: the cluster
could not be reached; there is no document, retry later. With --json it prints the verify document.
example:
defenseclaw substrate verify --install-file install.yaml

short: Say when one of your agents needs an answer or finishes its task
long:
Follows your agents (all of them, or the one you name) and prints a line when one raises an ask
or when a --task run ends. With notifications on (notifications.enabled and notifications.substrate in config.yaml),
it also shows a desktop notification, once per ask. A notification names the kind and the host or tool of an ask,
never its arguments. An administrator can turn notifications off for the cluster (substrate.activity.notifications: off).
Ctrl-C stops it.
